subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Climate Change and Tea
description: A short lesson to help you apply Climate Change and Tea.

hook.text: Darjeeling's prized first flush harvest is arriving earlier each year. Warming is changing tea's rhythm.

buildup.text: Tea plants are sensitive to temperature shifts. Even 1°C of change alters flavor compounds in the leaf.

discovery.text: Kenyan tea yields have dropped 20% in drought years. East Africa's tea belt is under growing pressure.

twist.text: Some regions may benefit. Higher altitudes and new latitudes could open up tea growing in unexpected places.

climax.text: Researchers are breeding heat-tolerant varieties, but terroir—the unique local character—can't be replicated.

punchline.text: Tea's flavor depends on place. Climate is rewriting the map.

quiz.question: How does warming affect tea?
options: It makes tea grow faster and better
Even small temperature shifts alter flavor compounds

details.summary: Climate change is altering rainfall patterns, increasing temperatures, and spreading pests in major tea-growing regions. Assam, Darjeeling, and parts of China and Kenya are experiencing reduced yields and changed flavor profiles. The tea industry faces challenges similar to coffee's climate crisis.
details.whyItMatters: Tea sustains millions of livelihoods. Climate-driven changes to yield and quality threaten both farming communities and the global tea supply.
takeaways: Erratic rainfall and rising temperatures affect tea yields
Flavor profiles are changing in traditional growing regions
Major tea regions including Assam and Darjeeling are at risk

faq.question: How does climate change affect tea flavor?
faq.answer: Higher temperatures can reduce the concentration of flavor compounds and catechins in tea leaves. Erratic rainfall disrupts the seasonal flush patterns that produce distinctive teas. Darjeeling's famous first flush is becoming less predictable. The teas of tomorrow may taste different.

faq.question: What is being done to protect tea from climate change?
faq.answer: Researchers are developing heat-tolerant tea cultivars. Farmers are adopting shade trees, water harvesting, and diversified cropping. Some regions are shifting to higher altitudes. However, an ancient tea bush takes years to establish, making adaptation slow.
